newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Campbell in $2.5 billion stock buy-back.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Campbell in $2.5 billion stock buy-back.

text.p: Like trying to squeeze more juice out of a ripe tomato, Campbell Soup Co. announced Thursday it would buy back stock, cut jobs and expand overseas in efforts to boost profits in the mature food industry.
"We are poised for breaking away from our competitors in the food industry," Chairman David W. Johnson said in announcing the initiatives to securities analysts in New York.

Campbell said it had authorized $2.5 billion in share repurchases, including a $1.5 billion "dutch auction," was planning to eliminate about 650 jobs, and would buy Erasco Group, the leading canned soup company in Germany.
Germany ranks as the largest commercial soup market outside the United States.

The announcements came a day after Campbell reported a sixth consecutive year of record sales and earnings. They follow a steady record of cost cutting under Johnson, who took over as Campbell president in 1990 and was named chairman in 1993.

The company said it will close or reorganize a number of manufacturing operations across North America, resulting in the elimination of 475 jobs. It will also cut 175 positions at its headquarters in Camden, N.J.
"Competition remains fierce," Johnson said, "so we must make strategic moves to maintain our leadership position and to grow Campbell to the next performance level."
Campbell's stock closed at $71-5/8, up $4.125, in late trading Thursday on the New York Stock Exchange Thursday.
Analysts said the moves had a good chance to pay off.
"The bottom line is that we expect earnings to improve," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Tim Ramey, in raising his rating on Campbell's stock to buy from hold.
Paine Webber analyst George Staphos said, "They hit on several themes that are important for food companies in terms of how they can control earnings over time."
"I think the prospects are good," he said.
Analysts said Johnson told a meeting in New York that Campbell aimed to steadily improve earnings while increasing sales growth from recent levels.
On Wednesday, Campbell said its profits rose by 15 percent to $802 million for the year ended July 28 as sales expanded by 6 percent to $7.68 billion.
"What he (Johnson) would like to see is sales growth on the order of 8 percent," said Fourteen Research analyst Sally Schaadt.
Ramey said earnings growth targets appeared to be around 15 percent to 16 percent annually.

Campbell said it would consolidate production of Ramen noodles -- closing an operation in Georgia -- sell poultry processing plants, end seasonal production of tomato paste at a plant in Sacramento, Calif., and make other changes to improve asset use.
These moves will result in an after-tax charge of about $160 million this fiscal year and will result in savings of $200 million over the next two years, Johnson said.

The company will also make a number of product and marketing changes to spur growth, he said. These include a new line of premium ready-to-serve soups, new frozen soups and faster roll-out of the Franco American Superiore range of premium canned pasta products.
In addition, Campbell announced plans to increase its advertising spending substantially, mainly for its soups, Pepperidge Farm snacks, V-8 vegetable juice and Swanson frozen foods.

Central to Johnson's strategy is his declared aim to move Campbell's financial performance into what he called the "Best of Show" category -- outpacing the entire food industry to perform in the top ranks of branded consumer goods firms.
This may be a tall order given the maturity of the industry, Schaadt said.

But plans to continue seeking expansion of the soup market -- such as through the introduction of a premium line of soups in glass jars -- indicate that Campbell is thinking along the right lines, she said.
"If the market itself can be expanded, he (Johnson) is going to get most of it," she said.
